title: Noncontrolling Interests: How to Report the Minority Share
summary: Noncontrolling interest accounting under ASC 810-10-45: where the minority share sits in equity, how income is attributed, and what a partner buyout does.
body_markdown:
## What Counts as a Noncontrolling Interest


Noncontrolling interest accounting is the US GAAP treatment of the slice of a consolidated subsidiary’s equity the parent doesn’t own. The ASC 810-10-20 glossary defines it as the portion of equity, or net assets, in a subsidiary not attributable, directly or indirectly, to a parent. Two structural tests decide whether your group has one at all, and indinero’s accounting team runs both before a number gets booked.


Control is the precondition. A noncontrolling interest exists only once the group has concluded it must consolidate, so a stake held without a controlling financial interest puts nothing in that column. That decision belongs to[equity method versus consolidation](https://www.indinero.com/blog/equity-method-vs-consolidation/) , along with the sub-50 percent side of it. The second test hides in two words: directly or indirectly. A parent owning 90 percent of Subsidiary J, where J owns 25 percent of Subsidiary N, holds an indirect 22.5 percent of N, and every equity interest outside that chain is a noncontrolling interest on consolidation.


### Only equity interests qualify


This gate disqualifies most of what a term sheet calls a minority stake. ASC 810-10-45-16A limits the treatment to equity-classified instruments, meaning an instrument or embedded feature issued by a subsidiary and classified as equity on the subsidiary’s own books, or one indexed to the stock of a consolidated subsidiary and classified as equity. ASC 810-10-45-17 closes the door from the other side: a liability-classified instrument isn’t a noncontrolling interest, because it isn’t an ownership interest.


Two questions settle it, and both answers have to be yes. Does the holder own legal-form equity in the subsidiary, and is that instrument classified as equity on the subsidiary’s own books? What fails the screen:


- **A profit share with no units.** An operating partner taking 20 percent of site-level profit under a management agreement is an expense through the income statement.
- **A service-vesting profits interest.** Vesting on continued employment points to compensation under ASC 718.
- **A subsidiary-level option or warrant.** Equity-classified, but not an outstanding share, so no income is attributed before exercise or expiration.
- **A management fee paid to the holder’s own entity.** A related-party expense.


One name for this is current GAAP, one is legacy. “Minority interest” is the pre-2009 label, and[FASB Statement No. 160](https://storage.fasb.org/fas160.pdf) replaced it throughout the Codification. These interests used to be reported as liabilities or in the mezzanine, and that diversity was eliminated in favor of presentation inside equity. Operators still search the older term, so both appear here.


## Where the Minority Share Sits on the Statements


Under ASC 810-10-45-15, the minority share sits inside consolidated equity, labeled separately from the parent’s equity. ASC 810-10-45-16 lets a group holding interests in more than one subsidiary present them in aggregate. That’s the whole answer to where minority interest on the balance sheet goes.


The ASC 810-10-45 noncontrolling interest presentation rules run from -15 through -21. Three of them are negative rules, and each is a defect a reviewer looks for.


- **Not a liability.** A “minority interest” line between total liabilities and total equity isn’t current GAAP for a nonredeemable interest.
- **Not in the mezzanine by default.** Temporary equity applies only to a redeemable interest in the scope of ASC 480-10-S99-3A, or where ASC 480 requires liability classification.
- **Not a deduction in reaching consolidated net income.** Earnings attributed to the interest are part of consolidated earnings, not a component of income or expense.


PwC’s financial statement presentation guide confirms the aggregation election ([PwC Viewpoint, Financial Statement Presentation Guide 2.5](https://viewpoint.pwc.com/content/pwc-madison/ditaroot/us/en/pwc/accounting_guides/financial_statement_/financial_statement___18_US/chapter_2_balance_sh_US/25_noncontrolling_in_US.html) ).


### The income statement, and why the bottom line misses the percentage


ASC 810-10-45-19 requires revenues, expenses, gains, losses, net income or loss, and other comprehensive income to be reported at consolidated amounts, which include the amounts attributable to the owners of the parent and to the noncontrolling interest. ASC 810-10-45-20 then attributes net income and comprehensive income to both. Consolidated revenue is 100 percent of the subsidiary’s revenue, and consolidated EBITDA is 100 percent of its EBITDA.


Ownership percentage does not scale any of it.


The split happens once, below consolidated net income, and ASC 810-10-50-1A(a) requires both attributable amounts on the face of the statements.


Consolidated income statement Amount


Net income 3,100


Less: net income attributable to noncontrolling interests (300)


Net income attributable to the parent 2,800


Earnings per share uses only the parent-attributable figure. A 70 percent owner reading that statement sees the full top line of a business they own 70 percent of, and a bottom line that isn’t 70 percent of anything. The figure matching their economics is net income attributable to the parent. Put both on the board deck and the question stops coming up.


### The roll-forward and the cash flow statement


ASC 810-10-50-1A(c) requires a reconciliation of total equity, parent equity, and noncontrolling interest equity from opening to closing, disclosing net income, owner transactions with contributions and distributions shown separately, and each component of other comprehensive income. ASC 810-10-50-1A(d) adds a note schedule showing the effect of any ownership change on parent equity.


The cash flow statement isn’t carved by ownership. Distributions to holders in their capacity as equity holders are financing outflows under ASC 230-10-45-15, as is cash paid to buy more of the interest while control is retained. A group under common control with no parent-subsidiary relationship presents[combined financial statements](https://www.indinero.com/blog/combined-financial-statements-common-control/) instead.


## Attributing Income and Loss Each Period


ASC 810-10-45-20 requires net income and comprehensive income to be attributed to the parent and the noncontrolling interest. It prescribes no method. Attributing net income to noncontrolling interest holders starts with the operating agreement, not the cap table.


What gets attributed is post-elimination consolidated income. ASC 810-10-45-18 provides that intra-entity income or loss to be eliminated isn’t affected by the existence of a noncontrolling interest, so the elimination runs in full first. Those entries live in[intercompany eliminations explained](https://www.indinero.com/blog/intercompany-eliminations-explained/) .


### The relative-ownership default, and what breaks it


The method has to be reasonable and appropriate to the circumstances. Substantive contractual provisions such as profit-sharing arrangements govern where they exist. Absent them, relative ownership applies, so a 60 percent controlling interest takes 60 percent of earnings.


Relative ownership is a default, not a rule.


The arrangements that break it, in rough order of frequency in a mid-market group:


- **A preferred return.** The first dollars of income belong to a priority claim, and only the residual follows the percentage.
- **A tiered distribution waterfall.** Return of capital, then preferred return, then a split that changes once a hurdle clears.
- **A priority allocation to the operating partner.** Drafted as an allocation rather than compensation, so it changes attribution instead of expense.


Deloitte’s roadmap works these cases in three steps: identify the contractual arrangements governing allocation and the priority of distributions, allocate current-period items on a basis other than ownership percentage, then allocate the residual so total allocations equal reported earnings. Each component of other comprehensive income follows the same method. Where the splits differ across financial reporting, taxation, distributions, and liquidation proceeds, the hypothetical liquidation at book value method may be appropriate if those splits are substantive. HLBV allocates on the change in each investor’s claim on net assets under the waterfall, and what it produces need not equal any percentage of consolidated net income.


### Losses, and the absence of a floor


ASC 810-10-45-21 reverses what a lot of experienced controllers learned first. Losses attributable to the parent and the noncontrolling interest may exceed their interests in the subsidiary’s equity, and the excess and any further losses are attributed to those interests, even when that produces a deficit balance ([Deloitte Roadmap, attribution of losses in excess of carrying amount](https://dart.deloitte.com/USDART/home/codification/broad-transactions/asc810-10/roadmap-noncontrolling-interests/chapter-6-attribution-income-other-comprehensive/6-3-attribution-losses-in-excess) ).


There is no floor at zero.


Open at 150 for a 30 percent holder, attribute 30 percent of a 1,000 subsidiary loss, and the interest closes at negative 150, presented inside equity as a negative. No reclassification to a receivable, because the holder has no funding obligation unless the agreement creates one. Distributions in excess of the carrying amount do the same thing. Check only whether a contractual arrangement, such as a parent guarantee of subsidiary debt, justifies a disproportionate allocation.


## When Ownership Changes Without Losing Control


Changes in a parent’s ownership that leave control intact are equity transactions under ASC 810-10-45-23. No gain or loss reaches consolidated net income or comprehensive income. ASC 810-10-45-22 covers every route, a parent buying more, a parent selling part of its stake, or the subsidiary reacquiring or issuing interests of its own. Initial measurement in a purchase price allocation is handled in[post-acquisition accounting and integration](https://www.indinero.com/blog/post-acquisition-accounting-integration/) .


### Buying out a minority shareholder accounting, in one entry


The group owns 70 percent of OpCo, whose book equity is $4,000,000 with no basis differences and no accumulated other comprehensive income, so the noncontrolling interest carries at $1,200,000. Buy another 10 percentage points from the operating partner for $700,000 in cash and the group moves to 80 percent, keeping control. The new carrying amount is 20 percent of $4,000,000, so the interest comes down by $400,000.


- Debit noncontrolling interests $400,000
- Debit additional paid-in capital $300,000
- Credit cash $700,000


PwC’s business combinations guide states the principle. Any difference between the adjustment to the noncontrolling interest and the consideration paid is recognized directly in equity and attributed to the controlling interest ([PwC Viewpoint, Business Combinations Guide 5.4](https://viewpoint.pwc.com/dt/us/en/pwc/accounting_guides/business_combination/business_combination__28_US/chapter_5_partial_ac_US/54_change-ownrshp.html) ).


So no goodwill for the $300,000 premium, and no gain or loss. OpCo’s assets aren’t remeasured, and only the attribution split moves prospectively. Transaction costs belong to the equity transaction, charged to equity rather than expensed. ASC 810-10-45-24 then requires accumulated other comprehensive income to be adjusted for the ownership change, through a charge or credit to parent equity. A sell-down reverses the whole entry, and the premium over book value still isn’t a gain. Only loss of control triggers remeasurement.


### When a put right enters the picture


A noncontrolling interest paired with a redemption feature is a redeemable noncontrolling interest, and the sequencing matters. ASC 480-10-S99-3A is an overlay applied after ASC 810-10, so classify the interest as equity first, then test whether it’s a redeemable equity security in scope. Three conditions put it there: the parent is an SEC registrant or has elected registrant guidance, the redemption feature isn’t a freestanding instrument under ASC 480 or ASC 815, and redemption isn’t solely within the issuer’s control.


Here’s the part that gets stated too strongly. A put right does not automatically push the balance into the mezzanine. ASC 480-10-S99-3A derives from SEC staff pronouncements including ASR 268, so a private non-registrant isn’t required to apply it and may elect to, and a later adoption is a change in accounting principle rather than an error correction. Mezzanine is the expected answer under most audit frameworks. For a private group it’s a documented accounting policy election, not an automatic GAAP outcome.


In scope, the interest sits in temporary equity at the maximum redemption amount if currently redeemable, with accretion or immediate remeasurement permitted under ASC 480-10-S99-3A(15) where redemption is probable but not current. Mandatory redemption is a separate test. ASC 480-10-25-4 classifies a mandatorily redeemable instrument as a liability unless redemption is required only on the liquidation or termination of the reporting entity. Liability, not mezzanine. Nonpublic non-registrants get a scope exception at ASC 480-10-15-7A and the paragraphs that follow.


None of this moves the tax filing. A 70 percent owned corporate subsidiary fails the 80 percent voting-power and value test in IRC 1504(a), so it files its own Form 1120 while being fully consolidated for GAAP. Which entity files what is a[business tax](https://www.indinero.com/services/business-tax-services/) question, not a consolidation one.


## Common Pitfalls


Every one of these turns up in diligence. Symptom, authority, fix.


1. **Shown as a liability, or in the mezzanine by default.** A line between total liabilities and total equity on a nonredeemable interest contradicts ASC 810-10-45-15, and FASB Statement No. 160 ended that diversity. Reserve temporary equity for interests in the scope of ASC 480-10-S99-3A.
2. **Its share of income shown as an expense line.** A “minority interest expense” line above net income makes consolidated net income already net of the minority share. ASC 810-10-45-19 and -20 want consolidated amounts first, attribution second, and ASC 810-10-50-1A(a) wants both on the face.
3. **The income statement scaled to the ownership percentage.** Consolidated revenue equal to 70 percent of OpCo’s revenue is proportionate consolidation, which isn’t permitted for a controlled subsidiary. Consolidate 100 percent, split once.
4. **Attribution on the percentage when the agreement says otherwise.** A 30 percent holder taking 30 percent of net income in a year a preferred return absorbed most of it fails the substance test behind ASC 810-10-45-20. Run the contractual allocations, then the residual.
5. **Loss attribution stopped at zero.** A balance parked at exactly zero across consecutive loss years is the old ARB 51 floor, which Statement 160 removed. The AICPA’s Journal of Accountancy put it in a line: the sharing of income or losses won’t be constrained,[even if it means reporting a deficit balance](https://www.journalofaccountancy.com/issues/2008/nov/noncontrollinginterestmuchmorethananamechange/) .
6. **A buyout booked as goodwill, or as a gain.** Debiting goodwill $300,000 for the premium above, rather than additional paid-in capital, violates ASC 810-10-45-23. So does a “loss on purchase of noncontrolling interest.” Reverse it to additional paid-in capital and add the ASC 810-10-50-1A(d) schedule.
7. **A put right nobody evaluated.** An interest in permanent equity while the shareholder agreement grants a put at a trailing EBITDA multiple needs a documented ASC 480-10-S99-3A scope conclusion plus the ASC 480-10-25-4 mandatory-redemption test. Read the shareholder agreement, not the cap table.
8. **A roll-forward that hasn’t tied since the partner came in.** Usually an unrecorded distribution, an unallocated OCI component, or an ownership-change adjustment booked straight to retained earnings. Rebuild the column with five movement types: opening balance, attributed income or loss, attributed OCI by component, contributions and distributions, and ownership changes. The close sequence that keeps it tied sits in the[multi-entity consolidation process](https://www.indinero.com/blog/multi-entity-consolidation-process/) .


These survive several closes because the balance sheet still foots. Two more to watch: a distribution to the minority holder sitting in operating cash flow belongs in financing, and a balance carried for a holder with no units usually means a profits interest or a management fee got misclassified.


## How Indinero Approaches Partially Owned Subsidiaries


Indinero’s accounting team is CPA-led and GAAP-first, which matters more here than on a clean single-entity close. Every question above is a judgment call documented in a memo, not a setting in a general ledger. The attribution basis. Whether a put right moves a balance into temporary equity. Whether a buy-in premium is additional paid-in capital or an error from three closes back.


Software doesn’t decide any of those.


The same 30 percent stake also produces three different answers in three places, which is the real argument for one team instead of three vendors. It’s a noncontrolling interest inside consolidated equity for GAAP. It breaks the 80 percent affiliated group test, so the subsidiary files its own return. And if it’s a pass-through, no provision is recorded on the noncontrolling interest’s share of its pretax income, so the consolidated effective tax rate lands below the parent’s statutory rate and someone on the board asks why. Bookkeeping, GAAP close, business tax, and fractional CFO advisory sit in one monthly engagement at indinero, the same engagement that covers the rest of your[multi-entity accounting](https://www.indinero.com/blog/multi-entity-accounting-guide/) .


What that produces on a partially owned subsidiary:


- **A written attribution policy per subsidiary** , tied to the operating agreement rather than the cap table, naming whether relative ownership, a waterfall, a preferred return, or HLBV governs.
- **A roll-forward that reconciles every period** , with the five movement types separated, so the ASC 810-10-50-1A(c) reconciliation and the (d) schedule come out of the close.
- **A read of each shareholder agreement** for redemption features, with the ASC 480-10-S99-3A scope conclusion and, for a private group, the policy election documented.

## Frequently asked questions


These seven come up on nearly every engagement with a partially owned subsidiary. They cluster around three things: how the minority stake is classified, how income and loss get attributed each period, and what happens when the group buys more of it. Each answer names the governing paragraph.


### Is a noncontrolling interest debt or equity?


A noncontrolling interest is equity, reported inside consolidated equity but clearly separate from the parent’s equity, under ASC 810-10-45-15 through -21. It isn’t a liability, and it isn’t in the mezzanine by default. Temporary equity is reserved for a redeemable interest within scope. Earnings attributed to the interest also aren’t a deduction in arriving at consolidated net income, so a minority interest expense line above net income is a defect a reviewer looks for.


### Do you still consolidate 100 percent of a subsidiary you only own 70 percent of?


Yes, consolidated revenue and expenses include 100 percent of a controlled subsidiary’s amounts regardless of ownership percentage, per ASC 810-10-45-19. The split happens once, below consolidated net income, as amounts attributable to the parent and to the noncontrolling interest under ASC 810-10-45-20. Scaling the income statement to 70 percent is proportionate consolidation, which isn’t permitted for a controlled subsidiary. Put consolidated net income and net income attributable to the parent side by side on the board deck.


### What happens when losses drive the noncontrolling interest balance negative?


Losses keep being attributed to the noncontrolling interest even after the balance goes negative, and the deficit is presented inside equity. ASC 810-10-45-21 is explicit that losses may exceed the holder’s interest in subsidiary equity, and the excess is still attributed. There’s no floor at zero. No reclassification to a receivable follows, because the holder owes nothing unless the agreement creates a funding obligation. A balance resting at exactly zero across loss years is the old ARB 51 floor.


### How is buying out a minority partner recorded?


Buying out part of a minority partner while keeping control is an equity transaction under ASC 810-10-45-23, with no gain or loss in income. Reduce the noncontrolling interest by the carrying amount of the percentage acquired, credit cash, and run the difference through additional paid-in capital. No goodwill for the premium, and no remeasurement of the subsidiary’s assets. Booking that premium as goodwill or as a gain is the most misbooked entry here, and indinero adds the ASC 810-10-50-1A(d) ownership-change schedule.


### Does a put right or buyback obligation change how the minority stake is classified?


A put right doesn’t automatically move the balance to temporary equity, because ASC 480-10-S99-3A comes from SEC staff guidance under ASR 268. A private non-registrant isn’t required to apply it and may elect to, and a later adoption is a change in accounting principle, not an error correction. Mezzanine is the expected answer under most audit frameworks, so indinero documents it as a policy election. Mandatory redemption is a separate test, and ASC 480-10-25-4 classifies a mandatorily redeemable instrument as a liability, not mezzanine.


### How are distributions to a minority owner presented?


Distributions to a minority owner are financing outflows on the consolidated statement of cash flows, and they reduce the noncontrolling interest balance in equity. ASC 230-10-45-15 treats cash paid to an equity holder in that capacity as a financing activity, and the same applies to cash paid to buy more of the interest while control is retained. Show contributions and distributions separately in the ASC 810-10-50-1A(c) equity reconciliation. A distribution sitting in operating cash flow is a common misclassification.


### Do noncontrolling interests change how the group files its tax return?


No, consolidated GAAP presentation of a noncontrolling interest changes nothing about which entity files which tax return. A 70 percent owned corporate subsidiary fails the 80 percent vote and value test in IRC 1504(a), so it files its own Form 1120 while being fully consolidated for GAAP. The practical effect shows up in the rate. If the subsidiary is a pass-through, no provision is recorded on the minority share of its pretax income, so the consolidated effective rate lands below the parent’s statutory rate.
